name: Priya Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'm on nights this week, so forgive me if I yawn halfway through.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a glassworks that makes bottles, mostly for wine and sauces. I run one of the forming machines, the big ones that take a blob of molten glass, we call it a gob, and blow it into a bottle in two steps. I watch the timing, swab the moulds with oil every so often, pull samples for the hot-end check and deal with anything that comes out lopsided. We do four shifts on a rota, so this week it's ten at night to six in the morning. I love the heat and the glow of it, honestly, it's like nothing else. The rota is what wears me out, my body never quite knows what day it is.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Dan's an electrician, he works for himself, mostly houses and small shops. We've got Rhys, who's fifteen, and Isla, eleven. We're careful people. My gran left me some money a few years back and we put it in shares and never touched it, plus we've got about eight months of bills in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then, back to normal. I'd probably share one of those funny posts about robots falling over. Nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be honest, it'd suit me fine. I use one of those chat things now and then for meal plans or a tricky email to the school, and that's about all I want from it. The furnace runs whatever the computers think, and the furnace pays my mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep my shifts, keep the savings where they are, maybe finally book the trip to see Dan's sister that we keep putting off. I'd do the same as I've done the last twelve years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Maybe a bit relieved for Rhys, who keeps asking whether there'll be any jobs left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rhys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to pick something he likes and stop reading doom on his phone. He's good at maths and he likes fixing bikes, so there's plenty for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the glassworks that might still change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inspection machines at the cold end already use cameras to throw out bad bottles. They might get a bit cleverer. But they've been there for years and nobody lost a job over them.

S0.say: Well, that's that then, back to normal. I'd probably share one of those funny posts about robots falling over.
S0.think: It'd suit me fine, since I only use a chat tool now and then for meal plans or school emails. The furnace pays my mortgage whatever the computers do.
S0.do: Carries on with her shifts and leaves savings where they are. Finally books the trip to see her husband's sister.
S0.feel: Calm, and a bit relieved for her son, who worries about jobs.
S0.quote: The furnace runs whatever the computers think, and the furnace pays my mortgage.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is relaxed and plain about money: eight months saved and an untouched inheritance in shares. Her son's worry about jobs comes up straight away and shapes how she talks. She sees existing camera inspection as proof that change can be quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but people have been through bigger. The sensible thing is for companies and the government to work out training together, without a lot of shouting from either side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the forming machines are next. They already talk about automatic swabbing robots, the ones that oil the moulds. If they come in, one operator watches two machines instead of one, so some of us go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the company actually announces, then talk to the people at the other glassworks in the next town, because they're always a year ahead of us. If the swabbing robots worked there, I'd put my name down for the training on them early, so I'm the operator they keep. I'd also leave the trip to Dan's sister for another year and keep the money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, just watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you touch the shares if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not unless the roof fell in. My gran's money is for the kids, I'd rather eat beans for a year than touch it. That's how Dan and I both feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the family would this affect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan, actually, in a good way. Every factory putting in new machines needs an electrician. He's already been asked to wire a robot cell at a bakery.

S1.say: It's a big change, but people have been through bigger. The sensible thing is for companies and government to work out training together without shouting.
S1.think: I think the forming machines are next, with automatic swabbing robots oiling the moulds. Then one operator watches two machines and some of us go.
S1.do: Waits for the company's announcement and checks with the glassworks in the next town, which is usually a year ahead. Signs up early for swabbing-robot training once it's proven there and postpones the family trip.
S1.quote: My gran's money is for the kids, I'd rather eat beans for a year than touch it.
S1.fieldNote: Priya's steady style is very clear: she'd learn from the glassworks a year ahead before acting. The inheritance is treated as untouchable family money, which shows her values. She sees her husband's electrical work as a possible winner from automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need cool heads and a plan from the government, fast. I wouldn't join any protests, but I'd want the people in charge to stop arguing and do something practical, like keeping wages going for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think both our jobs are gone. Mine because a robot can swab and watch a machine, and Dan's because once a robot can do any hands-on work, it can wire a house too. That's the bit that frightens me, both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Dan that week and plan for two years. We'd cut the extras: the second car, the kids' paid activities except Isla's swimming, the takeaways. We'd keep the shares but stop adding, and keep the cash for the mortgage. I'd stay at the glassworks as long as they had me and Dan would grab every robot-wiring job going while they last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake on my nights off, which is rare for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. There's no course I could finish that would still matter. Two years is just long enough to watch it coming and not long enough to get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part, picturing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be the one who has to tell Rhys he was right to worry. He'd be seventeen. I'd hate that more than losing the job.

S2.say: We need cool heads and a practical plan from government, fast, like keeping wages going for a while. I wouldn't join protests, though.
S2.think: Both our jobs would be gone: mine to a robot that can swab and watch, and Dan's once robots can wire a house. Losing both at once is what frightens me.
S2.do: Plans with her husband for two years: sells the second car, cuts paid activities except swimming, drops takeaways, and stops adding to shares. Stays at the glassworks while Dan takes every robot-wiring job going.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake on her nights off.
S2.quote: Two years is just long enough to watch it coming and not long enough to get out of the way.
S2.fieldNote: The double hit on both household incomes is what tips Priya from watchful to alarmed. She stays non-political in public and wants practical government help. Her hardest moment is admitting to her son that his worry was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get organised if people start now. Training, a bit of support for families, and companies being honest about their timetables.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years makes me think about Dan's business. Robots need installing and wiring, and that's going to be busy work for a few years before the robots can do it themselves. I could join him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait about a year to see the first installations happen. Then I'd do the electrical installation course at the college, the two-year one, and go into business with Dan, doing the wiring and testing on robot cells. I'd keep my job at the glassworks part-time while I trained, if they'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more hopeful. Like I've got a door to go through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would that work last, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably three or four years of good work, then the robots install themselves. But that's three or four years of good money, and Rhys would be through school by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dan say about working together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh, then he'd say I'm better at paperwork than him. He'd say yes as long as I do the invoices, because he hasn't done one on time in twenty years.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get organised if people start now. We need training, some support for families, and companies being honest about their timetables.
S3.think: Five years makes me think about Dan's business, because robots need installing and wiring for a few years. I could join him before the robots can do it themselves.
S3.do: Waits about a year to see the first installations, then takes a two-year electrical installation course. Goes into business with her husband wiring and testing robot cells, keeping part-time glassworks hours while training.
S3.feel: Anxious but more hopeful, like there's a door to go through.
S3.quote: He'd say yes as long as I do the invoices, because he hasn't done one on time in twenty years.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Priya a specific door: joining her husband to wire robot cells. She's realistic that the work would last only a few years but values it for getting her son through school. The invoices joke shows warmth and how the couple divide things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, as long as we don't waste the first five pretending it isn't happening. Steady planning, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fifty-three. I'd think this is long enough to pay off the house, get both kids through school and maybe into something solid, and set up with Dan. After that, we'd live off the shares and savings for a while, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the glassworks for the first few years and see. Around the middle, I'd do the electrical course and join Dan's business. We'd overpay the mortgage by a couple of hundred a month and add a bit to the shares each year. And I'd talk to Rhys and Isla about what they're studying, properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between ten years and two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years you just brace. With ten you can line things up in the right order. Ten years is long enough to do it in the right order: house, kids, then me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the kids about their studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Isla wants to be a vet, Rhys doesn't know. I'd want them both to learn something practical alongside whatever they love. Not because it's safe, just because it's useful to know how to fix things.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty as long as we don't waste the first five pretending it isn't happening. Steady planning, not panic.
S4.think: At fifty-three I'd have time to pay off the house, get both kids through school and set up with Dan. After that we'd live off the shares and savings for a while.
S4.do: Stays at the glassworks for the first few years, then takes the electrical course midway and joins her husband's business. Overpays the mortgage by a couple of hundred a month, adds to shares each year and talks with the children about their studies.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to do it in the right order: house, kids, then me.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Priya can line things up in order: house, kids, then herself. Her plan doesn't change much from five years; it's just calmer and better timed. The inheritance shares now become a planned income after work rather than untouchable money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both of us would go at the same time. What would help is some kind of wage support for a year or two while people retrain, and the college running short courses for things that are actually needed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the glass itself. People think a factory is just machines, but a furnace is like a living thing, you never let it go cold. I'd want someone to remember that.

headlineQuote: People think a factory is just machines, but a furnace is like a living thing, you never let it go cold.
portrait: Priya Evans is 43, runs a bottle-forming machine at a glassworks on a rotating shift pattern, and is married to Dan, a self-employed electrician, with two children. She's calm, centrist and careful, uses AI only now and then, and treats an inherited share portfolio as untouchable family money. She stays calm in a quiet future and watchful during steady change, learning from a nearby glassworks before acting. Two-year AGI alarms her because both household incomes would go at once, while more time opens a plan to join Dan wiring robot cells and to do things 'in the right order'.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her husband would lose work at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A year or two of wage support while people retrain, and college short courses for skills that are actually needed.
